items.answer: 200 words

items.stem: Nadia plans an essay on “How far should governments be able to restrict the media in the name of national security?” with this allocation: Introduction 10%, Perspective 1 and its evidence 25%, Perspective 2 and its evidence 25%, Comparison and evaluation 30%, Conclusion 10%, for 1,750 words. The first draft sections contain Introduction 115, Perspective 1 and its evidence 408, Perspective 2 and its evidence 558, Comparison and evaluation 525, Conclusion 255 words. Calculate the planned length of each section and the total length of the draft. State whether the draft is within the 1,750–2,000 word range.
items.answer: Planned: Introduction 175, Perspective 1 and its evidence 438, Perspective 2 and its evidence 438, Comparison and evaluation 525, Conclusion 175. Draft total = 1,861 words: within the range.

items.stem: Tomás plans an essay on “Should the permanent members of the UN Security Council lose their veto power?” with this allocation: Introduction 10%, Perspective 1 and its evidence 25%, Perspective 2 and its evidence 25%, Comparison and evaluation 30%, Conclusion 10%, for 1,800 words. The first draft sections contain Introduction 150, Perspective 1 and its evidence 530, Perspective 2 and its evidence 570, Comparison and evaluation 660, Conclusion 260 words. Calculate the planned length of each section and the total length of the draft. State whether the draft is within the 1,750–2,000 word range. Suggest which section should be revised first, and why.
items.answer: Planned: Introduction 180, Perspective 1 and its evidence 450, Perspective 2 and its evidence 450, Comparison and evaluation 540, Conclusion 180. Draft total = 2,170 words: 170 words over the limit. Revise the perspective 2 and its evidence first: it exceeds its plan by the most (120 words); keep the comparison/evaluation section strong as it carries most marks.
items.markingKey: 1 mark planned lengths; 1 mark draft total; 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark identifies section most over plan; 1 mark justification linked to purpose/marks [5]

items.stem: Evaluate the view that the structure of an essay matters more than the quality of its evidence.
items.answer: For: A clear structure makes comparison and evaluation visible to the reader. Signposting and topic sentences show the line of argument. Against: Without credible evidence, a well-structured essay is still unconvincing. Evaluation of sources is assessed directly. Judgement: Both are needed; e.g. an essay on “How far should governments be able to restrict the media in the name of national security?” needs structure to compare perspectives and evidence to support the judgement.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1–2 marks): simple, one-sided assertions with little support. Level 2 (3–4 marks): explains arguments on one side well, or both sides in less depth, using some evidence or examples. Level 3 (5–6 marks): balanced analysis of different perspectives, evidence evaluated for quality, and a reasoned, supported judgement on “to what extent”. [6]

items.stem: Explain why a thematic structure may be better than a “block” structure (one perspective, then the other) for an essay on “Should richer countries be banned from exporting plastic waste?”.
items.answer: A thematic structure compares perspectives point by point within each theme (e.g. effectiveness, rights, cost), so evaluation runs through the essay; a block structure risks two separate descriptions with comparison left to the end.

items.stem: A student writes: “After Ukraine introduced its ProZorro e-procurement system in 2016, many observers reported savings on public purchases. This proves that every government should publish all public contracts online.” Explain how the student could use this evidence more effectively.
items.answer: Explain how the evidence supports a reason (corruption thrives when deals are hidden from public view), comment on its credibility and whether it can be generalised, and acknowledge the counter-argument that publishing contracts could reveal commercially sensitive information; “proves” overstates what one example shows.
items.markingKey: 1 mark link evidence to reason; 1 mark evaluate source/generalisability; 1 mark avoid overstatement/consider counter-evidence [3]

items.stem: A student writes: “A 2019 study by the US National Institute of Standards and Technology found higher false-match rates for some demographic groups in many algorithms. This proves that governments should ban live facial recognition in public places.” Explain how the student could use this evidence more effectively.
items.answer: Explain how the evidence supports a reason (it records everyone, not only suspects), comment on its credibility and whether it can be generalised, and acknowledge the counter-argument that the technology helps police find missing people and dangerous suspects; “proves” overstates what one example shows.
items.markingKey: 1 mark link evidence to reason; 1 mark evaluate source/generalisability; 1 mark avoid overstatement/consider counter-evidence [3]

items.stem: Read this paragraph from an essay on “How far should governments be able to restrict the media in the name of national security?”: “Such laws are vague and let officials decide what is true. This suggests that these laws are more often used to silence critics than to protect the public. This supports the view that governments should repeal broad “false news” laws, although false reports can cause panic during a crisis.” Explain how the paragraph could show synthesis of evidence.
items.answer: Combine this evidence with a source from a different perspective, showing where they agree and differ, to build a more complete point.
items.markingKey: 1 mark combine sources; 1 mark explains agreement/difference [2]

items.stem: Read this paragraph from an essay on “Should richer countries be banned from exporting plastic waste?”: “Much exported plastic is not recycled but burned or dumped. This suggests that exporting waste shifts the harm onto poorer communities. This supports the view that richer countries should be banned from exporting plastic waste, although trade in sorted, clean plastic provides useful raw materials.” (a) Identify the element of a PEEL paragraph that is missing. (b) Write a sentence that would supply the missing element.
items.answer: (a) Evidence. (b) For example: After China’s 2018 import restrictions, Malaysia returned hundreds of containers of illegally imported plastic waste to their countries of origin.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark [1] (b) 1 mark relevant; 1 mark fits the paragraph [2]

items.stem: Hana argues that in an essay on the under-representation of women in parliaments, evaluating sources is more important than finding more evidence. How far do you agree? Support your answer with reasoning and evidence.
items.answer: For: Evaluation shows which evidence can be trusted and why. A few well-evaluated sources support stronger judgements than many unexamined ones. Against: Without enough evidence, perspectives cannot be compared fairly. Corroboration needs several sources. Judgement: Both matter; the best essays select a range of credible sources and evaluate them as they are used.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1–2 marks): simple, one-sided assertions with little support. Level 2 (3–4 marks): explains arguments on one side well, or both sides in less depth, using some evidence or examples. Level 3 (5–6 marks): balanced analysis of different perspectives, evidence evaluated for quality, and a reasoned, supported judgement on “to what extent”. [6]

items.stem: What is meant by “PEEL paragraph” in Global Perspectives?
options: Judging the strengths and weaknesses of arguments, evidence and sources.
Bringing together evidence from different sources to form a new, combined understanding.
Breaking an issue or argument into parts and explaining how they relate.
A paragraph structure: Point, Evidence, Explanation, Link back to the question.
items.answer: A paragraph structure: Point, Evidence, Explanation, Link back to the question.
items.markingKey: PEEL paragraph: a paragraph structure: Point, Evidence, Explanation, Link back to the question. [1]

items.stem: A student writes: “After Austria lowered the voting age to 16 in 2007, studies found that 16- and 17-year-olds turned out at rates similar to slightly older first-time voters. This proves that the voting age should be lowered to 16.” Explain how the student could use this evidence more effectively.
items.answer: Explain how the evidence supports a reason (16-year-olds will live longest with the results of today’s decisions), comment on its credibility and whether it can be generalised, and acknowledge the counter-argument that 16-year-olds are easily influenced by parents and teachers; “proves” overstates what one example shows.
items.markingKey: 1 mark link evidence to reason; 1 mark evaluate source/generalisability; 1 mark avoid overstatement/consider counter-evidence [3]

items.stem: Read this paragraph from an essay on “Are economic sanctions an effective way to change a government’s behaviour?”: “Targeted governments can blame foreigners for economic hardship. This suggests that sanctions often strengthen rather than weaken the targeted regime. This supports the view that economic sanctions are rarely an effective way to change a government’s behaviour, although sanctions helped end apartheid in South Africa.” Explain how the paragraph could show synthesis of evidence.
items.answer: Combine this evidence with a source from a different perspective, showing where they agree and differ, to build a more complete point.
items.markingKey: 1 mark combine sources; 1 mark explains agreement/difference [2]

items.stem: Read this paragraph from an essay on “Should governments be allowed to use live facial recognition in public places?”: “It records everyone, not only suspects. For example: A 2019 study by the US National Institute of Standards and Technology found higher false-match rates for some demographic groups in many algorithms. This supports the view that governments should ban live facial recognition in public places, although the technology helps police find missing people and dangerous suspects.” (a) Write a sentence that would supply the missing element. items.answer: (a) This suggests that the technology threatens the rights of innocent people. (b) Combine this evidence with a source from a different perspective, showing where they agree and differ, to build a more complete point.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark relevant; 1 mark fits the paragraph [2] (b) 1 mark combine sources; 1 mark explains agreement/difference [2]

It refuses to reach a judgement
It introduces a new argument not discussed in the essay
It overstates certainty and ignores limitations
items.answer: It only summarises the essay without answering the question

items.stem: A student’s conclusion reads: “In conclusion, it has been proved beyond doubt that economic sanctions are rarely an effective way to change a government’s behaviour, and nobody could disagree.” What is the main weakness?

It overstates certainty and ignores limitations

(b) Suggest one limitation the student could acknowledge.
items.answer: (a) It overstates certainty and ignores limitations. (b) e.g. sources mainly from one region, limited recent data, only two perspectives compared, or reliance on sources with vested interests.

items.stem: A student’s essay on “How effective are anti-corruption agencies at reducing corruption in government contracts?” ends: “In conclusion, there are good points on both sides about corruption in public procurement, so it is impossible to say.” (a) Suggest one limitation the student could acknowledge. items.answer: (a) e.g. sources mainly from one region, limited recent data, only two perspectives compared, or reliance on sources with vested interests. (b) e.g. How have attempts to create an independent anti-corruption agency with powers to prosecute worked in practice in different countries?
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark [1] (b) 1 mark relevant question; 1 mark linked to limitation [2]

items.stem: “A good conclusion to a Global Perspectives essay should always take a clear side.” Discuss this claim, considering arguments for and against before reaching a supported conclusion.
items.answer: For: The question asks for a judgement, so the conclusion must answer it. Sitting on the fence avoids the evaluation the essay has built up. Against: A qualified judgement (it depends on…) can be the most accurate answer. Limitations may mean certainty is not justified. Judgement: A conclusion should give a clear but qualified answer; e.g. on “Should social media companies be legally responsible for false political content on their platforms?”, stating the conditions under which each view holds.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1–2 marks): simple, one-sided assertions with little support. Level 2 (3–4 marks): explains arguments on one side well, or both sides in less depth, using some evidence or examples. Level 3 (5–6 marks): balanced analysis of different perspectives, evidence evaluated for quality, and a reasoned, supported judgement on “to what extent”. [6]

items.stem: A student’s conclusion reads: “In conclusion, the most important point, not mentioned earlier, is that data protection laws do not cover new technologies clearly.” What is the main weakness?
options: It only summarises the essay without answering the question
It refuses to reach a judgement
It introduces a new argument not discussed in the essay

items.stem: An essay on reform of the UN Security Council found that recent data were not available. Explain why the student should acknowledge this limitation in the conclusion.
items.answer: Because the situation may have changed since the sources were written, the judgement is less certain; acknowledging it shows critical awareness, makes the conclusion more credible and suggests further research.
items.markingKey: 1 mark effect of limitation on the judgement; 1 mark acknowledging shows reflection/credibility; 1 mark further research [3]

items.stem: A student’s essay on “Should the permanent members of the UN Security Council lose their veto power?” ends: “In conclusion, it has been proved beyond doubt that the veto power of the permanent members should be restricted, and nobody could disagree.” (a) Identify the main weakness of this conclusion. (b) Suggest one limitation the student could acknowledge.
items.answer: (a) It overstates certainty and ignores limitations. (b) e.g. sources mainly from one region, limited recent data, only two perspectives compared, or reliance on sources with vested interests.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark [1] (b) 1 mark [1]

items.stem: A student’s essay on “How far should governments be able to restrict the media in the name of national security?” ends: “In conclusion, there are good points on both sides about threats to press freedom, so it is impossible to say.” (a) Identify the main weakness of this conclusion. (b) Rewrite the conclusion so that it reaches a supported judgement. (c) Suggest one limitation the student could acknowledge.
items.answer: (a) It refuses to reach a judgement. (b) Overall, the evidence suggests that governments should repeal broad “false news” laws, mainly because such laws are vague and let officials decide what is true; however, this depends on the assumption that governments cannot be trusted to judge fairly what counts as false news, and the research relied mostly on sources from a few countries. (c) e.g. sources mainly from one region, limited recent data, only two perspectives compared, or reliance on sources with vested interests.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark [1] (b) 1 mark clear judgement; 1 mark supported by a reason from the essay; 1 mark qualified/limitation [3] (c) 1 mark [1]

I think that voting should be made compulsory.

items.stem: A student’s essay on “Should richer countries be banned from exporting plastic waste?” ends: “In conclusion, the most important point, not mentioned earlier, is that weak enforcement of waste rules in receiving countries.” (a) Suggest one limitation the student could acknowledge. (b) Suggest one question for further research.
items.answer: (a) e.g. sources mainly from one region, limited recent data, only two perspectives compared, or reliance on sources with vested interests. (b) e.g. How have attempts to ban exports and build domestic recycling capacity worked in practice in different countries?
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark [1] (b) 1 mark relevant question; 1 mark linked to limitation [2]

items.stem: “A good conclusion to a Global Perspectives essay should always take a clear side.” To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: For: The question asks for a judgement, so the conclusion must answer it. Sitting on the fence avoids the evaluation the essay has built up. Against: A qualified judgement (it depends on…) can be the most accurate answer. Limitations may mean certainty is not justified. Judgement: A conclusion should give a clear but qualified answer; e.g. on “Should the voting age be lowered to 16?”, stating the conditions under which each view holds.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1–3 marks): simple, one-sided assertions with little support. Level 2 (4–6 marks): explains arguments on one side well, or both sides in less depth, using some evidence or examples. Level 3 (7–9 marks): balanced analysis of different perspectives, evidence evaluated for quality, and a reasoned, supported judgement on “to what extent”. [9]

items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “the first sentence of a paragraph, stating its main point”?
items.answer: Topic sentence
items.markingKey: Topic sentence: the first sentence of a paragraph, stating its main point. [1]

items.stem: In an essay on “Should the voting age be lowered to 16?”, which section would do the following? “Explains the first perspective (e.g. a student union) with its reasoning and evidence.”
items.answer: Perspective 1 and its evidence
items.markingKey: Perspective 1 and its evidence. [1]

items.stem: Explain why a thematic structure may be better than a “block” structure (one perspective, then the other) for an essay on “Should social media companies be legally responsible for false political content on their platforms?”.
items.answer: A thematic structure compares perspectives point by point within each theme (e.g. effectiveness, rights, cost), so evaluation runs through the essay; a block structure risks two separate descriptions with comparison left to the end.
items.markingKey: 1 mark describes thematic; 1 mark describes block weakness; 1 mark explains benefit for comparison/evaluation [3]

items.stem: Hana plans a 1,750-word essay on “Should voting be made compulsory to increase democratic participation?”: Introduction 10%, Perspective 1 and its evidence 25%, Perspective 2 and its evidence 25%, Comparison and evaluation 30%, Conclusion 10%. How many words should the comparison and evaluation be?
items.answer: 525 words
items.markingKey: 30% × 1,750 = 525 words. 1 mark method, 1 mark answer [2]

items.stem: Omar is planning an essay on the question “Should the voting age be lowered to 16?”. Write a suitable opening sentence for the introduction.
items.answer: e.g. “Lowering the voting age to 16 is a global issue because different voting ages around the world, with Austria, Brazil and Argentina allowing voting at 16; this essay compares the perspectives of a student union and a conservative columnist.”
items.markingKey: 1 mark global context; 1 mark sets out perspectives [2]

items.stem: Tomás plans a 1,900-word essay on “How effective are anti-corruption agencies at reducing corruption in government contracts?”: Introduction 8%, Perspective 1 and its evidence 26%, Perspective 2 and its evidence 26%, Comparison and evaluation 30%, Conclusion 10%. How many words should the conclusion be?
items.answer: 190 words
items.markingKey: 10% × 1,900 = 190 words. 1 mark method, 1 mark answer [2]

items.stem: Evaluate the view that a good conclusion to a Global Perspectives essay should always take a clear side.
items.answer: For: The question asks for a judgement, so the conclusion must answer it. Sitting on the fence avoids the evaluation the essay has built up. Against: A qualified judgement (it depends on…) can be the most accurate answer. Limitations may mean certainty is not justified. Judgement: A conclusion should give a clear but qualified answer; e.g. on “Should governments be allowed to use live facial recognition in public places?”, stating the conditions under which each view holds.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1–2 marks): simple, one-sided assertions with little support. Level 2 (3–4 marks): explains arguments on one side well, or both sides in less depth, using some evidence or examples. Level 3 (5–6 marks): balanced analysis of different perspectives, evidence evaluated for quality, and a reasoned, supported judgement on “to what extent”. [6]

items.stem: Sipho argues that in an essay on corruption in public procurement, evaluating sources is more important than finding more evidence. How far do you agree? Support your answer with reasoning and evidence.
items.answer: For: Evaluation shows which evidence can be trusted and why. A few well-evaluated sources support stronger judgements than many unexamined ones. Against: Without enough evidence, perspectives cannot be compared fairly. Corroboration needs several sources. Judgement: Both matter; the best essays select a range of credible sources and evaluate them as they are used.

Level 3 (5–6 marks): balanced analysis of different perspectives, evidence evaluated for quality, and a reasoned, supported judgement on “to what extent”. [6]

items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “judging the strengths and weaknesses of arguments, evidence and sources”?
items.answer: Evaluation
items.markingKey: Evaluation: judging the strengths and weaknesses of arguments, evidence and sources. [1]

items.stem: Which sentence shows the best use of evidence in an essay on threats to press freedom?
options: A website says that these laws are more often used to silence critics than to protect the public.
Everyone knows that these laws are more often used to silence critics than to protect the public.
I think that governments should repeal broad “false news” laws.
According to a study by a university research centre with no funding from interested parties, which is credible because its authors have expertise and no obvious vested interest, …
items.answer: According to a study by a university research centre with no funding from interested parties, which is credible because its authors have expertise and no obvious vested interest, …
items.markingKey: It names the source and evaluates its credibility. [1]

items.stem: Which sentence shows the best use of evidence in an essay on the spread of online disinformation during elections?
options: I think that social media companies should be legally responsible for false political content.
According to a report by an intergovernmental organisation such as the UN Development Programme, which is credible because it draws on data from many countries and has a reputation to protect, …
A website says that platforms have both the power and the incentive to shape elections.
Everyone knows that platforms have both the power and the incentive to shape elections.
items.answer: According to a report by an intergovernmental organisation such as the UN Development Programme, which is credible because it draws on data from many countries and has a reputation to protect, …
items.markingKey: It names the source and evaluates its credibility. [1]

items.stem: Read this paragraph from an essay on “Should the permanent members of the UN Security Council lose their veto power?”: “A single country can block action supported by most of the world. This suggests that the veto prevents the Council from fulfilling its responsibility for international peace. This supports the view that the veto power of the permanent members should be restricted, although the veto keeps the great powers inside the UN system.” Write a sentence that would supply the missing element.
items.answer: For example: Russia has vetoed draft resolutions on the war in Syria many times since 2011.
items.markingKey: 1 mark relevant; 1 mark fits the paragraph [2]

items.stem: Read this paragraph from an essay on “Are gender quotas the best way to increase the number of women in parliament?”: “Voluntary efforts have increased women’s representation only slowly. For example: Rwanda’s constitution reserves 30% of seats for women, and women have held a majority of its lower house since 2008. This suggests that legal requirements are needed to change who is selected.” (a) Identify the element of a PEEL paragraph that is missing. (b) Write a sentence that would supply the missing element.
items.answer: (a) Link. (b) This supports the view that countries should introduce legal gender quotas for parliament, although quotas mean candidates are chosen because of gender rather than ability.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark [1] (b) 1 mark relevant; 1 mark fits the paragraph [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Which term matches this definition: “a final judgement that answers the question and follows from the arguments and evidence discussed”? (b) What is meant by “limitation” in Global Perspectives?
items.answer: (a) Supported conclusion (b) A weakness or restriction in the research, such as limited sources or a narrow focus.
items.markingKey: (a) Supported conclusion: a final judgement that answers the question and follows from the arguments and evidence discussed. [1] (b) Limitation: a weakness or restriction in the research, such as limited sources or a narrow focus. [1]

items.stem: A student’s conclusion reads: “This essay has looked at the government of Ethiopia and the government of Egypt and their views on disputes over shared rivers.” What is the main weakness?
options: It introduces a new argument not discussed in the essay
It refuses to reach a judgement
It overstates certainty and ignores limitations
It only summarises the essay without answering the question
items.answer: It only summarises the essay without answering the question
items.markingKey: It only summarises the essay without answering the question. [1]

items.stem: An essay on the spread of online disinformation during elections found that most sources came from high-income countries. Explain why the student should acknowledge this limitation in the conclusion.
items.answer: Because perspectives from the countries most affected may be missing, the judgement is less certain; acknowledging it shows critical awareness, makes the conclusion more credible and suggests further research.
items.markingKey: 1 mark effect of limitation on the judgement; 1 mark acknowledging shows reflection/credibility; 1 mark further research [3]

items.stem: A student’s essay on “Should richer countries be banned from exporting plastic waste?” ends: “In conclusion, it has been proved beyond doubt that richer countries should be banned from exporting plastic waste, and nobody could disagree.” (a) Identify the main weakness of this conclusion. (b) Suggest one limitation the student could acknowledge.
items.answer: (a) It overstates certainty and ignores limitations. (b) e.g. sources mainly from one region, limited recent data, only two perspectives compared, or reliance on sources with vested interests.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark [1] (b) 1 mark [1]

items.stem: A student’s essay on “Should voting be made compulsory to increase democratic participation?” ends: “In conclusion, the most important point, not mentioned earlier, is that voting procedures, such as having to vote in person on a working day, are inconvenient.” (a) Identify the main weakness of this conclusion. (b) Suggest one question for further research.
items.answer: (a) It introduces a new argument not discussed in the essay. (b) e.g. How have attempts to introduce automatic voter registration worked in practice in different countries?
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark [1] (b) 1 mark relevant question; 1 mark linked to limitation [2]
